title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: We grew up together with barely a year between our ages. We never knew disagreement or conflict. Harmony was the soul of our companionship. The differences in our characters only drew us closer. Elizabeth was calmer and more focused. But despite all my passion, I was capable of more intense concentration and was more deeply driven by a thirst for knowledge. She occupied herself with the imaginative creations of poets. In the magnificent scenery that surrounded our Swiss home — the towering mountains, the changing seasons, storms and calm, winter's silence, and the wild energy of our Alpine summers — she found endless sources of wonder and delight. While Elizabeth contemplated the grand appearance of things with a serious, satisfied spirit, I delighted in investigating their causes. The world was a secret I wanted to unlock. Curiosity, passionate research into nature's hidden laws, a joy close to rapture as they were revealed to me — these are among my earliest memories.

When my parents had a second son, seven years younger than me, they gave up their wandering life entirely and settled in their native country. We had a house in Geneva and a country estate at Belrive, on the eastern shore of the lake, a little more than three miles from the city. We lived mainly at the latter. My parents' lives were spent in considerable seclusion. My temperament led me to avoid crowds and attach myself deeply to a few people. I was indifferent to my schoolmates in general. But I formed the closest friendship with one of them. Henry Clerval was the son of a Geneva merchant. He was a boy of remarkable talent and imagination. He loved adventure, hardship, and even danger for its own sake. He was deeply read in books of chivalry and romance. He wrote heroic songs and began many tales of enchantment and knightly adventure. He tried to make us act out plays and pageants, with characters drawn from the heroes of Roncesvalles, where Roland and Charlemagne's knights made their last stand, King Arthur's Round Table, and the crusading knights who shed their blood to rescue the Holy Sepulchre, Christ's tomb in Jerusalem, from the hands of the infidels.

No one could have had a happier childhood than mine. My parents embodied kindness and indulgence. We felt they weren't tyrants ruling our lives by whim but the creators of all the delights we enjoyed. When I mixed with other families, I clearly saw how fortunate I was. Gratitude deepened my love for them.

My temperament was sometimes violent, and my passions intense. But by some quirk of nature, these energies weren't directed toward childish pursuits but toward an eager desire to learn — and not to learn everything randomly. I confess that neither languages, nor government, nor politics held any attraction for me. What I wanted were the secrets of heaven and earth. Whether it was the outward substance of things or the inner spirit of nature and the mysterious soul of man, my inquiries were always directed toward the metaphysical secrets of the world — or, in the highest sense of the word, its physical secrets.

Meanwhile, Clerval occupied himself with the moral dimensions of life. The busy stage of human affairs, the virtues of heroes, and the deeds of great men were his subjects. His hope and dream was to become one of those whose names are remembered as brave and generous benefactors of humanity. Elizabeth's saintly soul shone like a lamp in a shrine in our peaceful home. Her sympathy was ours. Her smile, her soft voice, the sweet light of her celestial eyes — these were always there to bless and uplift us. She was the living spirit of love, softening and attracting. I might have grown sullen in my studies or rough through the intensity of my nature, but she was there to soften me into something like her own gentleness. And Clerval — could anything have corrupted his noble spirit? Yet he might not have been so perfectly humane, so thoughtful in his generosity, so full of kindness and tenderness amid his passion for adventure, had she not shown him the true beauty of doing good and made it the highest aim of his ambition.

I take real pleasure in dwelling on memories of childhood, before misfortune poisoned my mind and turned its bright visions of being widely useful into gloomy, self-centered reflections. Besides, in painting the picture of my early days, I'm also tracing the events that led, step by invisible step, to my later tale of misery. When I try to account for the birth of the passion that came to rule my destiny, I find it rising like a mountain river from humble, nearly forgotten sources. But as it flowed onward, it swelled into a torrent that swept away all my hopes and joys.

Natural philosophy is the force that shaped my fate. So in this account, I need to explain what drew me to that science. When I was thirteen, we all went on a pleasure trip to the baths near Thonon. Bad weather forced us to stay indoors at an inn for a day. There I happened to find a volume of the works of Cornelius Agrippa, the sixteenth-century writer on magic and the occult. I opened it with little interest, but the theory he tries to prove and the wonderful facts he relates quickly filled me with excitement. A new light seemed to dawn on my mind. Bursting with joy, I told my father about my discovery. My father glanced casually at the title page and said, "Ah! Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, don't waste your time on this. It's worthless nonsense."

If instead of that dismissal my father had taken the time to explain that Agrippa's principles had been completely disproven — that modern science had far greater, real powers, while Agrippa's were imaginary — I would certainly have tossed Agrippa aside and satisfied my imagination, fired up as it was, by returning with greater enthusiasm to my previous studies. The entire course of my ideas might never have taken the fatal turn that led to my ruin. But his quick glance at my book didn't convince me he knew what was in it. I kept reading with the greatest eagerness.

When I got home, my first task was to get everything this author had written, and then the works of Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus. I read and studied the wild ideas of these writers with delight. They seemed like treasures known to few besides myself. I've described myself as always having a burning desire to penetrate nature's secrets. Despite the intense labor and wonderful discoveries of modern scientists, I always came away from my studies feeling dissatisfied. Isaac Newton reportedly said he felt like a child picking up shells beside the great unexplored ocean of truth. Those of his successors I knew of, in every branch of natural science, seemed to me — even with my boyish understanding — like beginners pursuing the same quest.

The uneducated farmer knew the elements around him and their practical uses. The most learned scientist knew little more. He'd partially unveiled Nature's face, but her immortal features remained a mystery. He could dissect, analyze, and name things. But even the secondary and tertiary causes of things — not to mention any final cause — were utterly unknown to him. I'd looked at the walls and barriers that seemed to keep humans from entering nature's fortress, and I'd foolishly resented them.

But here were books, and here were men who had penetrated deeper and knew more. I took them at their word and became their disciple. It may seem strange that this happened in the eighteenth century. But while I followed the standard curriculum in Geneva's schools, I was largely self-taught in my favorite subjects. My father wasn't a scientist, and I was left to struggle with a child's blindness combined with a student's thirst for knowledge. Under the guidance of my new teachers, I threw myself into the search for the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life. The latter soon captured my full attention. Wealth was a lesser goal. But imagine the glory of banishing disease from the human body and making people immune to everything but violent death!

These weren't my only fantasies. My favorite authors also promised the ability to summon ghosts and demons, a promise I eagerly pursued. When my attempts always failed, I blamed my own inexperience rather than any fault in my teachers. So for a time I was occupied with discredited systems, mixing a thousand contradictory theories together and floundering in a swamp of confused knowledge. I was guided only by a passionate imagination and childish reasoning — until an accident changed the direction of my thoughts.

When I was about fifteen, we were at our house near Belrive when we witnessed an incredibly violent thunderstorm. It came from behind the Jura mountains. Thunder crashed from every direction at once with terrifying force. I watched its progress with curiosity and delight. As I stood at the door, I suddenly saw a stream of fire shoot from an old, beautiful oak tree about twenty yards from our house. The moment the dazzling light vanished, the oak had disappeared. Nothing remained but a blasted stump. When we examined it the next morning, the tree had been shattered in a strange way — not splintered by the blast but reduced entirely to thin ribbons of wood. I'd never seen anything so utterly destroyed.

I already knew something about electricity. On this occasion, a man of great scientific knowledge was visiting us. Excited by what had happened, he explained a theory he'd developed about electricity and galvanism — the electricity produced by chemical action, famous for making the muscles of dead animals twitch. It was completely new and astonishing to me. Everything he said made Cornelius Agrippa, Albertus Magnus, and Paracelsus — the lords of my imagination — seem irrelevant. But by some twist of fate, the overthrow of these men killed my interest in pursuing my old studies. It seemed to me as if nothing could ever truly be known. Everything that had occupied me for so long suddenly felt worthless. In one of those sudden shifts of mind that we're perhaps most prone to in youth, I gave up my former interests entirely. I dismissed natural history and all its offshoots as a deformed and abortive creation and felt the greatest contempt for a so-called science that could never even step across the threshold of real knowledge. In this mood, I turned to mathematics and related subjects as being built on solid foundations and worthy of my attention.

How strangely our minds are made, and by what thin threads we're bound to prosperity or ruin. Looking back, it seems to me as if this almost miraculous change of direction was the last effort of my guardian angel to prevent the storm that was already gathering in the stars, ready to engulf me. Her victory was announced by an unusual calm and gladness of soul that followed my abandonment of my old studies, which had lately become a torment. I was being taught to associate evil with their pursuit and happiness with their neglect.
It was a strong effort of the spirit of good, but it was not enough. Destiny was too powerful, and her unchangeable laws had decreed my utter and terrible destruction.
